title: Non-teaching staff: welfare and recognition
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on looking after the cooks, security staff, cleaners, drivers, and other support staff who keep the school running.
body:
A school runs on more people than its teachers. Cooks, security guards, cleaners, groundsmen, drivers, matrons, and secretaries make daily school life possible, and they are often the least recognised members of the community.

Looking after them is both fair and practical. Support staff who are paid properly, treated respectfully, and safe at work tend to stay, take pride in their jobs, and protect the school.

Fair terms and proper pay

  • Written contracts that state duties, pay, and leave.
  • Pay on time, every month, without exception.
  • Statutory deductions and contributions done correctly and remitted.
  • Leave records kept, so entitlements are not argued about later.

Safety at work

Kitchen staff handle heat, knives, and food hygiene. Grounds staff use tools and chemicals. Security staff work nights. Provide protective gear, basic first aid training, and clear procedures. Food handlers need proper medical and hygiene checks.

Think about development too: Short training in first aid, food safety, or customer care helps support staff do their jobs and gives them skills that count, whatever happens next.

Give them a voice

Invite support staff representatives to relevant meetings, and ask what they need to do their jobs better. A cook may know more about storage problems than anyone else; a security guard may notice risks nobody else sees.

Recognise their contribution

Year-end is a natural time to say thank you. A simple recognition event, a certificate, or a mention at the closing assembly costs little and signals that the school sees their work.
